primary_topics: Chapter 5 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3) -- CJP's April 20, 2008 Inquirer column offering practical advice on how to pass (and top) the bar exams, a follow-up to his prior piece on the 'dismal' 2007 results and the need for the Supreme Court, the President and law schools to 'collaborate to produce better lawyers'

His self-deprecating handoff: feeling 'inadequate' because he 'placed only sixth' long ago, he gathered tips from three recent topnotchers -- Joan de Venecia (2005, UP), Arlene Maneja (2002, UST) and Mercedita Ona (2007, Ateneo)

Their common, practical tips -- believing one deserves to be there, honest self-evaluation and a realistic study plan, organizing materials, physical fitness, wise use of time, and abandoning emotional baggage and distractions

Craft-and-mindset advice -- perfect one's handwriting and grammar for human examiners, study 'smartly' from streamlined materials, master the basics, seek jurisprudence updates, and 'Pray. Pray. Pray.' -- with the closing reminder that 'there is no shortcut to passing the bar'
sub_topics: The setup: after his earlier column on the 'dismal' 2007 bar results urged the Court, the President and law schools to 'collaborate to produce better lawyers,' readers and 2008 reviewees pressed him for passing tips

The humble handoff: 'Having taken the exams eons ago,' and having 'placed only sixth,' CJP defers to topnotchers Joan de Venecia (2005), Arlene Maneja (2002, UST) and Mercedita Ona (2007, Ateneo) -- from UP, UST and Ateneo respectively

Mindset: 'Believe that you deserve to take the test,' forget past failures, and cultivate composure; do not compare yourself with others, since 'bar preparation is an individual task' and understanding matters more than rote readings

Planning: make time for 'serious self-evaluation' of strong and weak subjects and budget days accordingly; keep a realistic study plan and organized materials (e.g., 'eight separate boxes or drawers' by subject) so no time is lost hunting for notes

Self-care and realism: be 'kind to yourself' (allow rest and fun, since the bar is hard enough), and stay physically fit -- exercise, nourishing meals, sleep, vitamins and stress management -- lest 'your body bogs down'

Using time and classes wisely: attend review lectures if you already know a subject, but read up first if you do not (since classes assume a baseline), and save 'bar tips' for the pre-week; abandon emotional problems, enlist family support, and avoid distractions

Craft: 'perfect your handwriting and grammar,' because examiners are 'only human' and reward readable, logical answers -- all three topnotchers credit good penmanship; visual learners should write out notes

Substance and spirit: 'study smartly' from streamlined materials (codal provisions, a good reviewer, jurisprudence updates), 'master the basics' and their application (even via 'audio codals' while traveling), 'ask for updates' since doctrines change and questions are facts-based, and 'Pray. Pray. Pray.' -- for in the end 'there is no shortcut,' so focus only on what you can control and on 'positive thinking'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3), CJP's April 20, 2008 Inquirer column, is a practical guide on how to pass -- 'nay, top' -- the bar exams, following up his earlier piece on the 'dismal' 2007 results and the need for the Supreme Court, the President and law schools to 'collaborate to produce better lawyers.' Feeling 'inadequate' because he 'placed only sixth' long ago, he hands the advice to three recent topnotchers -- Joan de Venecia (2005, UP), Arlene Maneja (2002, UST) and Mercedita Ona (2007, Ateneo) -- and relays their common tips. On mindset: believe you deserve to be there, forget past failures, cultivate composure, and do not compare yourself with others, since 'preparation is an individual task' and understanding beats rote memorization. On planning: make time for 'serious self-evaluation,' budget days by subject, keep a realistic plan, and organize materials (even 'eight separate boxes' by subject) so no time is lost. On self-care: be 'kind to yourself,' allow rest, and stay physically fit -- exercise, sleep, nourishing meals, vitamins and stress management -- lest the body give out. On time: attend review classes for subjects you know but read up first on those you do not, and save 'bar tips' for the pre-week, while abandoning emotional baggage and distractions. On craft: 'perfect your handwriting and grammar,' since examiners are 'only human' and reward readable, logical answers (a point all three topnotchers credit), and write out notes if you learn visually. On substance: 'study smartly' from streamlined materials (codal provisions, a good reviewer, jurisprudence updates), master the basics and their application (even via 'audio codals' on the road), ask for updates since doctrines change and questions are facts-based, and 'Pray. Pray. Pray.' His final reminder: 'there is no shortcut to passing the bar' -- put in the hours, ignore what you cannot control like 'examiners' or 'kinds of questions,' and devote your energy to studying and 'positive thinking.'
